photos.question: A client is prescribed oral potassium chloride extended-release tablets. Which instruction should the nurse include?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #357!

🍌 Potassium pills can hurt the stomach if taken the wrong way. Do you know the rule?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Swallow it whole with food and plenty of water

🧠 Rationale: Oral potassium irritates the stomach and esophagus.

Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the whole dose at once.

Salt substitutes contain potassium and can push levels too high.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Potassium Chloride (Oral)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Electrolyte replacement

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Low potassium (hypokalemia)

🔹 Often given with loop or thiazide diuretics

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Nausea, stomach upset

🔹 GI irritation or ulcers

🔹 High potassium if overdosed

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check potassium and kidney function

✅ Give with food and a full glass of water

✅ Do not crush extended-release tablets

✅ Teach to avoid salt substitutes unless approved

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Potassium pill? Whole, with food, with water!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #Pharmacology #Potassium #Electrolytes #MedSafety #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: The nurse listens to the heart and hears the second sound (the "dub" in lub-dub). What causes this sound?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #358!

🫀 Lub-dub! Do you know which valves make the dub?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Closing of the aortic and pulmonic valves

🧠 Rationale: S2 (dub) happens when the aortic and pulmonic valves close.

It marks the end of systole and the start of diastole.

S1 (lub) is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heart Sounds

❤️ S1 (Lub):

🔹 Mitral and tricuspid valves close

🔹 Start of systole

🔹 Loudest at the apex

❤️ S2 (Dub):

🔹 Aortic and pulmonic valves close

🔹 Start of diastole

🔹 Loudest at the base

⚠️ Extra Sounds:

🔹 S3: may mean heart failure

🔹 S4: stiff ventricle, like long-term high BP

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Listen with the diaphragm for S1 and S2

✅ Report new extra sounds or murmurs

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

S1 = AV valves shut. S2 = Semilunar valves shut. 1 before 2, A before S!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #CardiacNursing #HeartSounds #Assessment #Cardiology #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis needs an insulin infusion. Which type of insulin can be given intravenously?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #359!

💉 Only one of these insulins belongs in an IV bag. Which one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Regular insulin

🧠 Rationale: Regular insulin is the standard insulin for IV infusions in DKA.

NPH is cloudy and is never given IV.

Glargine and detemir are long-acting and given subcut only.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Types

⚡ Rapid-Acting:

🔹 Lispro, aspart, glulisine

🔹 Give with meals

💧 Short-Acting:

🔹 Regular insulin

🔹 Clear, the main insulin used IV

☁️ Intermediate:

🔹 NPH, cloudy

🔹 Subcut only

🕐 Long-Acting:

🔹 Glargine, detemir, degludec

🔹 Steady basal coverage, do not mix

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check potassium before starting the drip

✅ Check glucose every hour on an infusion

✅ Use an infusion pump

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Regular rides the IV road!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

photos.question: A newborn is born with clubfoot. Which treatment is usually started first?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #360!

🦶 A newborn's foot turns in and down. What is the first step to fix it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Serial casting soon after birth

🧠 Rationale: Treatment starts early, often in the first 1 to 2 weeks.

Casts are changed about weekly to slowly correct the foot.

A brace is then worn for several years to prevent relapse.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Clubfoot (Talipes Equinovarus)

👶 What It Is:

🔹 Foot turned inward and downward

🔹 Can affect one or both feet

🩹 Treatment:

🔹 Serial casting (Ponseti method)

🔹 Often a small heel cord release

🔹 Foot abduction brace afterward

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check toes for color, warmth and movement

✅ Keep the cast clean and dry

✅ Report swelling or cool, pale toes

✅ Teach parents brace routine

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Clubfoot? Cast early, cast often, then brace!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #Pediatrics #PedsNursing #Clubfoot #Orthopedics #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: A client at 10 weeks of pregnancy has vomiting many times a day, weight loss and ketones in the urine. What should the nurse suspect?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #361!

🤰 This is more than normal morning sickness. Can you name it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Hyperemesis gravidarum

🧠 Rationale: Normal morning sickness does not cause weight loss or ketones.

Hyperemesis causes dehydration and electrolyte problems.

Preeclampsia and gestational diabetes usually appear after 20 weeks.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperemesis Gravidarum

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Vomiting many times a day

🔹 Weight loss of 5% or more

🔹 Ketones in urine, dehydration

🩸 Labs to Watch:

🔹 Potassium and sodium

🔹 Urine specific gravity

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ IV fluids and antiemetics as ordered

✅ Daily weights, intake and output

✅ Small, frequent bland meals once tolerated

✅ Offer emotional support

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Hyperemesis = hyper vomiting + weight loss + ketones!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #Maternity #OBNursing #Pregnancy #WomensHealth #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: A client who often feels angry starts lifting weights at the gym every day to release that anger. Which defense mechanism is this?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #362!

🏋️ Turning anger into gym time. Which defense mechanism is it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Sublimation

🧠 Rationale: Sublimation turns strong feelings into a positive, accepted activity.

Displacement would be taking the anger out on a safer target.

Sublimation is considered a healthy, mature defense.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Defense Mechanisms

🧠 Common Ones:

🔹 Sublimation: feelings into healthy activity

🔹 Displacement: feelings onto a safer target

🔹 Projection: blaming others for your own feelings

🔹 Repression: unconsciously blocking memories

✅ Healthy vs Unhealthy:

🔹 Sublimation and humor are mature

🔹 Denial and projection can block coping

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Notice the behavior without judging

✅ Encourage healthy coping skills

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Sublimation = Sweat it out in a Socially accepted way!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #MentalHealth #PsychNursing #DefenseMechanisms #Psychiatry #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: A client with a head injury has a new fixed, dilated right pupil. What does this finding most likely suggest?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #363!

👁️ One pupil just blew after a head injury. What does it mean?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Rising ICP pressing on cranial nerve III

🧠 Rationale: Rising pressure in the skull can press on cranial nerve III.

This makes the pupil on that side fixed and dilated.

Opioids cause small (pinpoint) pupils, not dilated ones.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pupils and Increased ICP

⚠️ Signs of Rising ICP:

🔹 Change in LOC (earliest sign)

🔹 Fixed, dilated pupil (late sign)

🔹 Cushing triad: high SBP, low HR, irregular breathing

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Notify the provider right away

✅ Head of bed 30 degrees, head midline

✅ Frequent neuro checks

✅ Avoid coughing, straining and hip flexion

🚑 Emergency:

🔹 A blown pupil can mean brain herniation

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Blown pupil = brain pressure. Call it in NOW!
